section_summary: This section records a dispute over how far Japan should rebuild its merchant fleet and shipbuilding industry after the war. State Department officials weigh Japan’s economic needs against American shipping interests’ objections, while American and Chinese shipowners urge restrictions on Japanese overseas trade. The final despatch reports progress in repairing Japan’s existing vessels and the continuing difficulty of keeping them in service.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Need for an Overseas Merchant Marine
subfiles.from: V. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Concludes an argument for allowing Japan an overseas merchant marine.
subfiles.summary: Sebald argues that an unarmed Japan needs economical ocean transport for trade and recovery and that merchant shipping alone would not threaten world peace.

subfiles.title: SCAP Message on American Flag Carriage of Cargo for Japan
subfiles.about: Explains how American flag vessels are considered for ore, coal and other cargo bound for Japan.
subfiles.summary: SCAP describes recent ore carriage, coal procurement and its policy for assigning cargo purchased with United States funds.

subfiles.title: Coordination of Policy on the Japanese Merchant Marine
subfiles.about: Reviews consultations and changing United States proposals for Japanese fleet and shipbuilding levels.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum traces interagency discussions from wartime restrictions through proposals to enlarge Japanese shipbuilding capacity and merchant tonnage. It says other offices were informed, while classified negotiations and pending foreign shipbuilding contracts complicated broader consultation.

subfiles.title: Request for Hearing on the Japanese Merchant Marine
subfiles.about: Calls for a coordinated Department position before meeting American shipping representatives.
subfiles.summary: Norton forwards the shipping federation’s request and warns that American industry, Congress and other governments may oppose rapid Japanese fleet expansion. He urges consultation among State Department offices, with Lovett if needed.

subfiles.title: Future Status of the Japanese Merchant Marine
subfiles.about: Assesses substantive and procedural objections to rebuilding Japanese shipping.
subfiles.summary: Allison argues that artificial restrictions would conflict with occupation policy and cites Japan’s depleted, aging fleet. He supports a Department meeting before wider consultation and recommends waiting for a fuller report from Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Japanese Merchant Marine
subfiles.from: Frazer A. Bailey, National Federation of American Shipping
subfiles.about: Opposes an immediate return of the Japanese merchant fleet to its prewar size.
subfiles.summary: Bailey argues that a four million ton Japanese fleet would threaten American shipping interests without materially improving Japan’s finances. He disputes historical balance of payments figures, cites Japanese subsidies and uncertainty about future trade, and proposes confining Japanese vessels chiefly to domestic and nearby routes. He asks to present further views before policy is settled.

subfiles.title: U.S. Policy on Japanese Shipping
subfiles.about: Records a State Department meeting on Japanese shipping policy and industry consultation.
subfiles.summary: Participants agreed to draft a policy history and position before meeting American shipping representatives.

subfiles.title: Request for an Informal Conference on Japanese Shipping
subfiles.about: Renews the federation’s request to discuss Japanese merchant shipping with State Department representatives.
subfiles.summary: Bailey encloses Draper’s reply and asks Saugstad to arrange an informal conference.

subfiles.title: Reply to Frazer A. Bailey
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Bailey’s views and directs requests concerning the Far Eastern Commission to State.
subfiles.summary: Draper says the Army will retain the letter for study, send a copy to SCAP and refer FEC matters to State.

subfiles.title: Japanese Merchant Marine, Attached Copy
subfiles.from: Frazer A. Bailey, National Federation of American Shipping
subfiles.about: Reproduces Bailey’s detailed objection to rapid Japanese merchant fleet expansion.
subfiles.summary: This attached copy repeats the letter on pages 267–279. It challenges the economic case for a four million ton fleet, describes Japanese shipping subsidies and uncertain postwar trade, and urges restrictions on overseas operations pending better evidence and consultation.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Letter Protesting Restoration of Japanese Merchant Marine
subfiles.about: Forwards a Chinese shipowners’ protest addressed to the American shipping federation.
subfiles.summary: The embassy transmits Chinese and English copies without endorsement and leaves the decision whether to forward the private letter to the Department.

subfiles.title: Chinese Text of Protest Against Restoration of Japanese Merchant Marine
subfiles.about: Presents the Chinese shipowners’ opposition to restoring Japan’s merchant fleet.
subfiles.summary: The Chinese-language enclosure supports the American federation’s protest and calls for limits on Japanese ships and reparations for China. Its corresponding English text follows.

subfiles.title: Protest Against Restoration of Japanese Merchant Marine
subfiles.about: Supports the federation’s protest and proposes strict limits on Japanese shipping.
subfiles.summary: The association asks that Japan’s fleet be limited to one million tons and confined to coastal trade. It seeks Japanese vessels and shipbuilding equipment as reparations, American help for Chinese shipping and an early peace conference.

subfiles.title: Protest Against Restoration of Japanese Merchant Marine, Hectograph Copy
subfiles.about: Reproduces the English text of the Chinese shipowners’ protest.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the request for a one million ton Japanese fleet, a ban on overseas trade, reparations for China and a peace conference.

subfiles.title: Nanking’s Despatch No. 456
subfiles.about: Recommends returning the Chinese association’s private letter rather than forwarding it through government channels.
subfiles.summary: The writer warns that forwarding it could imply State Department sympathy with its position.

subfiles.title: Chinese Reaction to American Shipping Federation Letter
subfiles.about: Reports Chinese shipowners’ concern over revived Japanese competition on nearby routes.
subfiles.summary: The despatch says Chinese shipowners oppose Japanese access to the Korea, Formosa, Philippines and Asian mainland routes they hope to develop. It encloses the association’s protest.

subfiles.title: Protest Against Restoration of Japanese Merchant Marine, Consular Copy
subfiles.about: Reproduces the Chinese shipowners’ letter opposing restoration of Japan’s merchant fleet.
subfiles.summary: The copy repeats demands for coastal-only Japanese trade, a one million ton fleet and reparations for China.

subfiles.title: Forwarding Press Release Regarding Repairs to Japanese Merchant Marine Vessels
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a SCAP release on Japanese merchant vessel repairs.
subfiles.summary: The despatch notes a 25–30 percent repair ratio and a goal of 15 percent.

subfiles.title: SCAP Reports Progress in Repair of Merchant Marine
subfiles.from: Far East Command Public Information Office
subfiles.about: Reports repair and salvage efforts for Japan’s merchant fleet.
subfiles.summary: The release attributes extensive repairs to old and wartime-built ships, inexperienced crews and shortages. A joint committee aims to reduce the repair ratio to about 15 percent, while salvage and major repairs return vessels to service.
